entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 28 Is 28:1-29 . The twenty-eighth through thirty-third chapters form almost one continuous prophecy concerning the destruction of Ephraim, the impiety and folly of Judah, the danger of their league with Egypt, the straits they would be reduced to by Assyria, from which Jehovah would deliver them on their turning to Him; the twenty-eighth chapter refers to the time just before the sixth year of Hezekiak's reign, the rest not very long before his fourteenth year. 1. crown of pride-- Hebrew for "proud crown of the drunkards," &c. [Horsley], namely, Samaria, the capital of Ephraim, or Israel. "Drunkards," literally ( Is 28:7 , 8 ; Is 5:11 , 22 ; Am 4:1 ; 6:1-6 ) and metaphorically, like drunkards, rushing on to their own destruction. beauty ... flower-- "whose glorious beauty or ornament is a fading flower." Carrying on the image of "drunkards"; it was the custom at feasts to wreathe the brow with flowers; so Samaria, "which is (not as English Version, 'which are') upon the head of the fertile valley," that is, situated on a hill surrounded with the rich valleys as a garland ( 1Ki 16:24 ); but the garland is "fading," as garlands often do, because Ephraim is now close to ruin (compare Is 16:8 ); fulfilled 721 B.C. ( 2Ki 17:6 , 24 ).

Rather, "the fading flower, their glorious beauty (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.1">Is 28:1</reference>), which is on the head of the fat (fertile) valley, shall be as the early fig" [G. V. Smith]. Figs usually ripened in August; but earlier ones (Hebrew bikkurah, Spanish bokkore) in June, and were regarded as a delicacy (<reference osisRef="Jer.24.2">Jr 24:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.9.10">Ho 9:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.7.1">Mi 7:1</reference>).<div eID="gen14655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14656" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">while it is yet--</hi>that is, immediately, without delay; describing the eagerness of the Assyrian Shalmaneser, not merely to conquer, but to destroy utterly Samaria; whereas other conquered cities were often spared. <div eID="gen14656" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8815"/><div sID="gen14676" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8815"/><hi type="bold">15. said--</hi>virtually, in your conduct, if not in words.<div eID="gen14676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14677" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">covenant--</hi>There may be a tacit reference to their confidence in their "covenant" with the Assyrians in the early part of Hezekiah's prosperous reign, before he ceased to pay tribute to them, as if it ensured Judah from evil, whatever might befall the neighboring Ephraim (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.1">Is 28:1</reference>). The full meaning is shown by the language ("covenant with death--hell," or sheol) to apply to all lulled in false security spiritually (<reference osisRef="Ps.12.4">Psa 12:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.8">Ec 8:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.8.11">Jr 8:11</reference>); the godly alone are in covenant with death (<reference osisRef="Job.5.23">Job 5:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.2.18">Ho 2:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.22">1Co 3:22</reference>).<div eID="gen14677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14678" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">overflowing scourge--</hi>two metaphors: the hostile Assyrian armies like an overwhelming flood.<div eID="gen14678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14679" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pass through--</hi>namely, through Judea on their way to Egypt, to punish it as the protector of Samaria (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.4">2Ki 17:4</reference>).<div eID="gen14679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14680" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lies--</hi>They did not use these words, but Isaiah designates their sentiments by their true name (<reference osisRef="Amos.2.4">Am 2:4</reference>). <div eID="gen14680" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 15. said-- virtually, in your conduct, if not in words. covenant-- There may be a tacit reference to their confidence in their "covenant" with the Assyrians in the early part of Hezekiah's prosperous reign, before he ceased to pay tribute to them, as if it ensured Judah from evil, whatever might befall the neighboring Ephraim ( Is 28:1 ). The full meaning is shown by the language ("covenant with death--hell," or sheol) to apply to all lulled in false security spiritually ( Psa 12:4 ; Ec 8:8 ; Jr 8:11 ); the godly alone are in covenant with death ( Job 5:23 ; Ho 2:18 ; 1Co 3:22 ). overflowing scourge-- two metaphors: the hostile Assyrian armies like an overwhelming flood. pass through-- namely, through Judea on their way to Egypt, to punish it as the protector of Samaria ( 2Ki 17:4 ). lies-- They did not use these words, but Isaiah designates their sentiments by their true name ( Am 2:4 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8816"/><div sID="gen14681" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8816"/>16. Literally, "Behold Me as Him who has laid"; namely, in My divine counsel (<reference osisRef="Rev.13.8">Re 13:8</reference>); none save I could lay it (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.5">Is 63:5</reference>).<div eID="gen14681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14682" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stone--</hi>Jesus Christ; Hezekiah [Maurer], or the temple [Ewald], do not realize the full significancy of the language; but only in type point to Him, in whom the prophecy receives its exhaustive accomplishment; whether Isaiah understood its fulness or not (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.11">1Pe 1:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">12</reference>), the Holy Ghost plainly contemplated its fulfilment in Christ alone; so in <reference osisRef="Isa.32.1">Is 32:1</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Gen.49.24">Ge 49:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.118.22">Psa 118:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.21.42">Mt 21:42</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.10.11">Ro 10:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.20">Ep 2:20</reference>.<div eID="gen14682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14683" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tried--</hi>both by the devil (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.1-Luke.4.13">Lu 4:1-13</reference>) and by men (<reference osisRef="Luke.20.1-Luke.20.38">Lu 20:1-38</reference>), and even by God (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.46">Mt 27:46</reference>); a stone of tested solidity to bear the vast superstructure of man's redemption. The tested righteousness of Christ gives its peculiar merit to His vicarious sacrifice. The connection with the context is, though a "scourge" shall visit Judea (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.15">Is 28:15</reference>), yet God's gracious purpose as to the elect remnant, and His kingdom of which "Zion" shall be the center, shall not fail, because its rests on Messiah (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.24">Mt 7:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.7.25">25</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.19">2Ti 2:19</reference>).<div eID="gen14683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14684" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">precious--</hi>literally, "of preciousness," so in the Greek, (<reference osisRef="1Pet.2.7">1Pe 2:7</reference>). He is preciousness.<div eID="gen14684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14685" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">corner-stone--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Kgs.5.17">1Ki 5:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.7.9">7:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.38.6">Job 38:6</reference>); the stone laid at the corner where two walls meet and connecting them; often costly.<div eID="gen14685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14686" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">make haste--</hi>flee in hasty alarm; but the Septuagint has "be ashamed"; so <reference osisRef="Rom.9.33">Ro 9:33</reference>, and <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.6">1Pe 2:6</reference>, "be confounded," substantially the same idea; he who rests on Him shall not have the shame of disappointment, nor flee in sudden panic (see <reference osisRef="Isa.30.15">Is 30:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.32.17">32:17</reference>). <div eID="gen14686" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8823"/><div sID="gen14701" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8823"/>23. Calling attention to the following illustration from husbandry (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.1">Psa 49:1</reference>, 2). As the husbandman does his different kinds of work, each in its right time and due proportion, so God adapts His measures to the varying exigencies of the several cases: now mercy, now judgments; now punishing sooner, now later (an answer to the scoff that His judgments, being put off so long, would never come at all, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.19">Is 5:19</reference>); His object being not to destroy His people any more than the farmer's object in threshing is to destroy his crop; this vindicates God's "strange work" (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.21">Is 28:21</reference>) in punishing His people. Compare the same image, <reference osisRef="Jer.24.6">Jr 24:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.2.23">Ho 2:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.3.12">Mt 3:12</reference>. <div eID="gen14701" type="x-p"/>

This also--</hi>The skill wherewith the husbandman duly adjusts his modes of threshing is given by God, as well as the skill (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.26">Is 28:26</reference>) wherewith he tills and sows (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.24">Is 28:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.25">25</reference>). Therefore He must also be able to adapt His modes of treatment to the several moral needs of His creatures. His object in sending tribulation (derived from the Latin tribulum, a "threshing instrument," <reference osisRef="Luke.22.31">Lu 22:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.5.3">Ro 5:3</reference>) is to sever the moral chaff from the wheat, not to crush utterly; "His judgments are usually in the line of our offenses; by the nature of the judgments we may usually ascertain the nature of the sin" [Barnes]. <chapter eID="Isa.28"/>

navigation_sections.title: CHAPTER 28
navigation_sections.content_plain: CHAPTER 28 Is 28:1-29 . The twenty-eighth through thirty-third chapters form almost one continuous prophecy concerning the destruction of Ephraim, the impiety and folly of Judah, the danger of their league with Egypt, the straits they would be reduced to by Assyria, from which Jehovah would deliver them on their turning to Him; the twenty-eighth chapter refers to the time just before the sixth year of Hezekiak's reign, the rest not very long before his fourteenth year.
